topic: How to give feedback that changes behaviour, not just feelings

facts.statement: Effective feedback names a specific, observed behaviour, a particular action at a particular time, rather than a trait or a general judgement of the person.
Effective feedback states the concrete impact that behaviour had, such as an effect on the work, the team, or a deadline.
Effective feedback ends with a question that invites the other person's view of what happened, turning a one way verdict into a two way conversation.
The feedback conversation closes with an agreed next step, so both people know what will be repeated or changed going forward.
Feedback aimed at a trait or at the person as a whole tends to trigger defensiveness, because it reads as a judgement of character rather than a description of what happened.
facts.caveat: This is a widely observed pattern in workplace communication guidance rather than a single controlled finding; treat it as a well established tendency, not a fixed rule for every person.

facts.statement: Vague feedback does not specify which action to repeat or stop, so even a person who wants to improve does not know which behaviour to change next time.
facts.caveat: Widely taught as the reason vague feedback fails to change action, drawn from workplace communication practice rather than a single named study.

facts.statement: Naming a specific behaviour and its impact gives the receiver a concrete, repeatable or changeable unit of action instead of an abstract label about who they are.
facts.caveat: This is the commonly stated rationale for behaviour and impact framing in workplace feedback guidance, not a single controlled result.

facts.statement: A trait or judgement framing uses labels about the person's character or attitude, while a behaviour framing describes one observable, specific action, and this distinction is the basis for the whole shape.

A widely taught structure for this shape, naming the situation, the behaviour and the impact, is commonly attributed to the Center for Creative Leadership as its Situation-Behaviour-Impact (SBI) model.
facts.caveat: The attribution to the Center for Creative Leadership is commonly cited in workplace training materials; I can confirm the model's name and the attribution as widely repeated, but not verify a specific original publication or date, so the lesson should present it as a commonly used name for the shape rather than a cited research finding.
facts.reference_hint: Commonly attributed to the Center for Creative Leadership (CCL), as the Situation-Behaviour-Impact model

facts.statement: The feedback sandwich, opening and closing a criticism with praise, is a commonly used technique but is not considered best practice for changing behaviour, because wrapping the specific behaviour and impact in praise can dilute or obscure the one thing the receiver needs to act on.
facts.caveat: This is a widely shared critique in workplace feedback guidance rather than a single controlled study; the technique remains common in practice even where it is discouraged.

not_claimed: Any statistic or percentage about feedback effectiveness, retention, or behaviour change (no real named source is grounded here)
Learning styles or VARK style matching
The feedback sandwich presented as best practice for changing behaviour
A specific controlled study proving the SBI model outperforms other feedback formats
Any HR, disciplinary, or formal performance review procedure
A specific publication date, author, or direct quote from the Center for Creative Leadership
scope_note: Covers the everyday shape of behaviour-change feedback between colleagues (specific behaviour, concrete impact, question, agreed next step) and why vague or person directed feedback tends to change feelings but not the next action. Excludes HR process, performance reviews, and any statistic without a real named source.
